title: Module 3 Interpretation Check
intro: Each item gives you a short research situation. Decide what the evidence supports.

items.q: A study finds r = +.62 between hours studied and exam score. What proportion of exam score variability is accounted for by study time in this linear relationship?
items.why: .62 squared = .384. The other roughly 62 percent comes from everything else, including prior knowledge and test conditions.

items.q: Ice cream sales and drownings are positively correlated across months. What best explains this?
o: A third variable, warm weather, likely drives both
The correlation must be a calculation error
items.why: Season is a classic confounding variable. A correlation alone cannot separate these explanations.

items.q: Five scores have SS = 40. What is the sample variance?
items.why: Variance = SS divided by (n minus 1) = 40/4 = 10. Dividing by n would give 8, which is the population formula.

items.q: A scatterplot shows a clear U shape and the correlation is r = .02. What should you conclude?
o: A strong relationship exists, but it is not linear, so r misses it
items.why: Pearson r detects only straight line patterns. Always plot your data.

items.q: A researcher says, "My correlation was r = −.45, so something went wrong because the effect should be positive." What is the best reply?
o: A negative r is not an error. It means one variable tends to go down as the other goes up
The sign does not matter at all
Take the absolute value and ignore the direction
items.why: The sign tells you the direction. A negative correlation can be perfectly meaningful, for example more practice and fewer errors.
